Warm Up: Predator-Prey System — Sketching a Solution Curve

Sketch an approximate solution to the system of first-order differential equations with the given initial value:

\[\begin{cases} \dfrac{dx}{dt} = -5x + 5xy \\[8pt] \dfrac{dy}{dt} = 35x - 5xy \end{cases} \qquad x(0) = 1,\quad y(0) = 7\]
Diagram description: A vector field is displayed on a grid with the \(x\)-axis ranging from \(-1\) to \(10\) and the \(y\)-axis from \(-1\) to \(10\). The blue arrows show the direction \((dx/dt,\, dy/dt)\) at each lattice point. In the left portion of the field (small \(x\)), arrows point nearly straight upward; as \(x\) increases, arrows rotate to point rightward and then curve downward in the upper-right region. The pattern is consistent with closed orbits (periodic solutions) around an interior equilibrium, typical of Lotka–Volterra-type predator-prey systems. The initial condition \((1,\, 7)\) is in the upper-left region of the field.

Page 4

Systems of First Order ODEs — Motivation

The world around us gives us systems of first order ODEs. Examples include:

  • Mixing Tanks
  • Predator-Prey
  • SIR
  • Spring-Mass Systems

Big Idea: Turn second-order ODEs into systems of first-order ODEs.

Page 5

Spring-Mass Model — Physics Background

Page description: This page presents the physical setup for the spring-mass model. A diagram shows a mass \(m\) attached to a horizontal spring. The mass can move left and right along the \(x\)-axis. Key variables and physical quantities are introduced: \(x(t)\) denotes the displacement of the mass from its natural (equilibrium) position at time \(t\), and \(v(t) = \dot{x}(t)\) is the velocity. Newton’s second law is applied: the net force equals mass times acceleration. For a spring obeying Hooke’s Law, the restoring force is \(F = -kx\), where \(k > 0\) is the spring constant. The resulting second-order ODE is \(m\ddot{x} = -kx\), or equivalently \(\ddot{x} = -\frac{k}{m}x\).

Spring-Mass System (Hooke’s Law): Let \(x(t)\) be the displacement from equilibrium and \(v(t) = \dot{x}(t)\) the velocity. Newton’s second law with a spring restoring force gives:

\[m\ddot{x} = -kx \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \ddot{x} = -\frac{k}{m}\,x\]

Conversion to first-order system: Introducing \(v = \dot{x}\), the second-order ODE becomes the equivalent first-order system:

\[\begin{cases} \dot{x} = v \\[4pt] \dot{v} = -\dfrac{k}{m}\,x \end{cases}\]

Page 6

Spring-Mass Model — Physics (continued)

Page description: This page continues the physical derivation of the spring-mass system. The handwritten notes develop the system further, discussing how the phase portrait of the system \(\dot{x} = v,\; \dot{v} = -(k/m)x\) consists of closed elliptical orbits centered at the origin \((0,0)\), corresponding to periodic (oscillatory) motion of the spring-mass system. The equilibrium at the origin is a center — a stable but not asymptotically stable equilibrium where nearby solutions orbit indefinitely without spiraling in or out.

The equilibrium \((0,\, 0)\) of the undamped spring-mass system is a center: solutions orbit around it in closed ellipses. This corresponds to perpetual oscillation of the mass, with no energy lost.

Page 7

Spring-Mass Model — Exercise: Sketching the Phase Portrait

Sketch an approximate solution to the spring-mass system with the given initial value:

\[\begin{cases} \dfrac{dx}{dt} = v \\[8pt] \dfrac{dv}{dt} = -0.18x \end{cases} \qquad x(0) = 0,\quad v(0) = 3\]
Diagram description: A vector field is shown in the \(xv\)-plane (displacement \(x\) on the horizontal axis, velocity \(v\) on the vertical axis), both axes ranging from \(-5\) to \(5\). The arrows form a characteristic elliptical rotation pattern: in the upper half (\(v > 0\)) arrows point to the right (since \(\dot{x} = v > 0\)), and in the right half (\(x > 0\)) arrows point downward (since \(\dot{v} = -0.18x < 0\)). This produces a counterclockwise rotation, consistent with closed elliptical orbits around the origin. Starting from \((0,\, 3)\) (on the positive \(v\)-axis), the solution would travel rightward and downward, tracing a closed ellipse around the origin.

Page 8

Spring-Mass Model — Example Phase Portrait

System (undamped spring-mass):

\[\begin{cases} \dfrac{dx}{dt} = v \\[8pt] \dfrac{dv}{dt} = -0.15x \end{cases}\]
Diagram description: A phase portrait labeled “Spring-Mass System” is shown in the \(xv\)-plane. The horizontal axis is labeled “Displacement (x)” and ranges from \(-4\) to \(4\); the vertical axis is labeled “Velocity (v)” and ranges from \(-4\) to \(4\). Blue arrows fill the plane indicating the vector field. A single red closed elliptical orbit is drawn, labeled “Trajectory (3, 0)”, starting from the initial condition \((3,\, 0)\). The ellipse is wider along the \(x\)-axis than the \(v\)-axis, reflecting the asymmetry introduced by the coefficient \(-0.15\). The trajectory circles the origin counterclockwise, confirming the equilibrium at \((0,\, 0)\) is a center.

Page 9

Spring-Dashpot-Mass Model — Physics Background

Page description: This page introduces the damped spring-mass (spring-dashpot-mass) model. A diagram shows a mass \(m\) attached to both a spring (providing restoring force \(-kx\)) and a dashpot (a damping device providing a force proportional to velocity, \(-bv\), where \(b > 0\) is the damping coefficient). Newton’s second law now gives: \(m\ddot{x} = -kx - b\dot{x}\). The notes explain the physical meaning of each term: the spring term \(-kx\) pulls the mass back toward equilibrium, and the dashpot term \(-bv\) resists motion, dissipating energy.

Spring-Dashpot-Mass System: With spring constant \(k > 0\) and damping coefficient \(b > 0\):

\[m\ddot{x} = -kx - b\dot{x}\]

Equivalent first-order system: Setting \(v = \dot{x}\):

\[\begin{cases} \dot{x} = v \\[4pt] \dot{v} = -\dfrac{k}{m}\,x - \dfrac{b}{m}\,v \end{cases}\]

Page 10

Spring-Dashpot-Mass Model — Example Phase Portrait

System (damped spring-mass):

\[\begin{cases} \dfrac{dx}{dt} = v \\[8pt] \dfrac{dv}{dt} = -0.15x - 0.1v \end{cases}\]
Diagram description: A phase portrait labeled “Spring-Mass System” is shown in the \(xv\)-plane with axes from \(-4\) to \(4\) on both. Blue arrows fill the plane. A red spiral trajectory starting from \((3,\, 0)\) winds inward counterclockwise toward the origin, growing smaller with each loop. This contrasts sharply with the closed ellipses of the undamped case; here the damping term \(-0.1v\) causes energy to dissipate, so the mass eventually comes to rest at the equilibrium.

The dashpot term \(-0.1v\) introduces damping and changes the qualitative behavior: the trajectory spirals inward instead of forming a closed ellipse.

Therefore \((0,\, 0)\) is a spiral sink (stable spiral equilibrium): all nearby solutions spiral toward the origin as \(t \to \infty\).

Page 11

Numerical Approximations — Euler’s Method for Systems (Setup)

Page description: This page sets up Euler’s method for numerically approximating solutions to the spring-mass system. The handwritten notes recall the general Euler’s method update rule for a two-dimensional system \(\dot{x} = f(x,v)\), \(\dot{v} = g(x,v)\):

Euler’s Method for the Spring-Mass System:

\[x_{n+1} = x_n + f(x_n,\, v_n)\,\Delta t = x_n + v_n\,\Delta t\] \[v_{n+1} = v_n + g(x_n,\, v_n)\,\Delta t = v_n + (-0.18\,x_n)\,\Delta t\]

Starting from initial conditions \(x_0\) and \(v_0\), each step produces the next approximate state. The step size \(\Delta t = 0.1\) is used in the accompanying spreadsheet.

Page 13

Parametric Curves

Definition: A parametric curve is a rule from time \(\mathbb{R}\) to points in the phase plane \(\mathbb{R}^2\):

\[\vec{F}(t) = \begin{bmatrix} f(t) \\ g(t) \end{bmatrix} = \langle f(t),\, g(t) \rangle\]

where the left form is column notation and the right form is row notation.

Here \(f\) is the horizontal component and \(g\) is the vertical component. As \(t\) varies, we sweep out a path in the plane.

Page 14

Parametric Curves — Examples

“Graphs”

The parametric curve \(\vec{F}(t) = \begin{bmatrix} t \\ g(t) \end{bmatrix}\) traces the graph of \(g\) as a function of \(t\). As \(t\) increases, the point moves along the curve of \(g\).

Diagram description: A small coordinate system is sketched with horizontal axis \(t\) and vertical axis labeled \(g(t)\). An orange curve rises from left to right, labeled “graph of \(g\)”.

Circles / Ellipses

The parametric curve \(\vec{F}(t) = \begin{bmatrix} a\cos(t) \\ b\sin(t) \end{bmatrix}\) traces an ellipse (or circle when \(a = b\)) in the plane.

Diagram description: A small sketch shows an ellipse with arrows indicating the direction of travel as \(t\) increases (counterclockwise).

Spirals

The parametric curve \(\vec{F}(t) = \begin{bmatrix} a\,t\cos(t) \\ b\,t\sin(t) \end{bmatrix}\) traces a spiral that grows outward from the origin as \(t\) increases.

Diagram description: A small sketch shows a spiral expanding outward from the origin, with an arrow indicating the direction of increasing \(t\).
